name: The mental map at the top
idea: The work argues that top managers run a diversified firm through a dominant logic: a shared mental map of the business and of how to manage it, formed by experience in the core business. It argues that a diversified firm's performance depends on whether its businesses can be run with that logic, so that strategic variety among them, not only their spread of products, sets the limit.
suggests: Look at whether a company's businesses can be run with the way of thinking that grew up in its core business, or whether some need a different one.
limits: The work allows that a top team can hold more than one dominant logic, though only a limited number, so a firm need not confine itself to businesses that share a single logic.
competing_idea: Another view holds that managers use cash beyond what profitable projects need to make diversifying acquisitions, which grow the firm they run but tend to destroy value.
questions: Is the newest business run with the same assumptions and management tools as the core business?
Do the businesses differ in what it takes to win, even where their products look related?
Is top management's experience drawn mainly from one business?

originals.reference: C. K. Prahalad and Richard A. Bettis, "The dominant logic: A new linkage between diversity and performance", Strategic Management Journal, Vol. 7 No. 6, November 1986, pp. 485-501
Michael C. Jensen, "Agency Costs of Free Cash Flow, Corporate Finance, and Takeovers", American Economic Review, Vol. 76 No. 2, 1986, pp. 323-329
